At 4:17 in the morning, the refrigerator began to hum in a different key.

Mara woke because the sound had changed. Usually it was a tired, practical hum, the sound of a machine doing its small duty in the dark. This was lower, almost musical. It seemed to come from beneath the floorboards as much as from the kitchen.

She lay still, listening.

The apartment was old enough to have opinions. Pipes knocked when nobody used water. The hallway bulb flickered only when Mara was sad, though she had told herself many times that this was coincidence. The windows trembled before storms, sometimes hours before the weather forecast caught up. So the refrigerator singing was not, by itself, impossible.

She rose, wrapped herself in the yellow robe her aunt had given her, and walked barefoot into the kitchen.

The refrigerator stood in the corner with its door slightly open.

Mara stopped.

She always closed it. She was the sort of person who checked the lock twice, who turned the stove knobs even after she had not cooked, who carried umbrellas on cloudless days. An open refrigerator door was not a thing that happened around her.

Cold light spilled across the tiles.

Inside, between a jar of mustard and a carton of eggs, sat a small blue door.

It was no taller than a book. It had a brass knob. Frost gathered along its edges, delicate as lace.

Mara stared at it for a long time.

Then she said, “No.”

The little door remained where it was.

“No,” she repeated, more firmly.

From behind it came the faint sound of someone laughing.

That was worse.

Mara shut the refrigerator, pressed both hands against its cool metal surface, and took a breath. Her life had been strange lately in quiet ways. A bird had flown into her apartment one afternoon, circled the ceiling fan without touching it, and left through the same closed window it had entered. A woman on the bus had called Mara by her childhood nickname, one nobody had used in twenty years. Last Tuesday, she had found a silver button in her coat pocket, though she owned no silver coat.

Still, a door in the refrigerator felt excessive.

She made coffee. She put bread in the toaster. She opened the refrigerator again for milk.

The blue door was gone.

In its place was a note, folded into a neat square and tucked beneath the butter dish.

Mara did not touch it until after breakfast.

The note was written in green ink.

COME HOME, it said.

There was no signature.

Mara read it four times. Then she laughed, once, sharply, because she had lived in this apartment for nine years and had no other home to return to.

Her parents were dead. Her sister lived three states away and communicated mostly through photographs of her dog. The town where Mara had grown up had changed its name after a flood, or perhaps before one; she could never remember. The old house had been sold, demolished, replaced by a pharmacy with a bright red sign. There was nowhere to go.

And yet, all day, the note followed her.

At work, it appeared in the margin of a spreadsheet, though when she blinked it was only a streak of green highlighter. On the train, an advertisement for vacations had the word HOME printed in large blue letters. A child in a red hat looked up at Mara and said, “You missed the turn.”

His mother apologized. “He’s been saying odd things all week.”

“That’s all right,” Mara said.

But it was not all right.

That evening, she did not turn on the lights. She sat by the kitchen window while the city darkened itself building by building. Across the street, someone practiced scales on a piano. Somewhere below, a dog barked with the solemnity of a person giving testimony.

Mara took the folded note from her pocket.

Come home.

She thought of the house where she had grown up: the cracked green paint on the porch, the smell of rain in the hallway, the impossible number of spiders in the basement. She thought of her mother singing while she washed dishes, never quite remembering the words to any song. She thought of being seven years old and certain that the moon followed her because it had chosen her specifically.

Perhaps home, she thought, was not a place. Perhaps it was a time. Perhaps it was a person. Perhaps it was a trap.

At 11:03, the refrigerator began to hum again.

Mara stood.

This time, when she opened the door, the blue door was waiting.

The brass knob was warmer than it should have been.

Behind her, the kitchen clock ticked once, twice, and then stopped.

Mara opened the little door.

There was no tiny room beyond it. There was a staircase descending through darkness. It was absurdly large, impossible to fit inside the refrigerator. Wind rose from below, carrying smells of wet grass, cinnamon, dust, and something like old books.

She should have closed the door.

She should have called someone. Her sister, perhaps. The police. A plumber.

Instead, Mara climbed in.

The staircase seemed to take hours, though she could still hear the refrigerator humming somewhere above her. The steps were made of wood worn smooth in the center, as if generations of feet had passed over them. On the walls hung framed photographs, but each one was blank until Mara walked by. Then images appeared.

Her first day of school.

Her father asleep in an armchair.

A birthday cake with seven candles.

A train station she had never seen.

A woman she did not recognize, standing beneath an orange tree.

Mara stopped before the last photograph.

The woman looked directly at her. She had Mara’s eyes, though older, clearer somehow. In the photograph, she raised one hand and touched the glass from the other side.

“Who are you?” Mara whispered.

The woman’s mouth moved.

Mara leaned closer.

The answer came not as sound, but as memory: I am the part of you that stayed.

The stairs ended at a field beneath a purple dawn.

Mara stood in tall grass silvered with dew. Ahead was a house with a green porch and a crooked chimney. Smoke rose from it. The windows glowed gold.

She knew this house.

Not exactly. The porch was wider. The garden was full of flowers her mother had always wanted to plant but never did. A bicycle leaned against the fence. On the roof sat three black crows, watching her with bright, patient eyes.

The front door opened.

Her mother stood there, younger than Mara remembered her, wearing an apron dusted with flour.

“Mara,” she called. “You’re late.”

For one bright, unbearable second, Mara believed.

Then she saw the grief in her mother’s face. Not grief for herself. Grief for Mara.

“You can’t stay,” her mother said gently.

Mara’s throat closed.

“I know,” she said.

Her mother nodded, as if this were a lesson they had practiced many times. “But you can visit. That’s different.”

Behind Mara, the staircase waited in the grass.

Her mother stepped forward and kissed Mara’s forehead. She smelled of cinnamon and rain.

“Go on,” she said. “You have a life upstairs.”

Mara wanted to say that her life was small. That it was full of unpaid bills, lonely dinners, fluorescent offices, and mornings when getting out of bed felt like lifting a house. She wanted to say that nobody had waited for her in years.

But then she remembered the child on the train. The piano across the street. Her sister’s dog, ridiculous and beloved. The yellow robe. The coffee waiting to be made. The chance, however tiny, that tomorrow might contain something she had not yet imagined.

So Mara walked back up the stairs.

When she emerged, dawn was entering the kitchen.

The refrigerator door was closed. The blue door was gone.

On the counter lay a single silver button.

Mara picked it up and smiled.

Then she made coffee for two, just in case.
